name: Brunei Malay
confidence_why: Clynes 2001, the only first-hand statement on Brunei Malay proper, says there is no published description of its stress and only that prominence "appears" penultimate; Soderberg 2014 reports penultimate stress for a Kedayan speaker from Sabah (a dialect), Deterding & Ishamina 2017 give no stress section, and Clynes & Deterding 2011 found no lexical stress at all in the Standard Malay of Brunei, so whether Brunei Malay has word stress and where it falls has never been established.
catalog_citation: Clynes, Adrian. 2001. Brunei Malay: An overview. Occasional Papers in Language Studies, Department of English Language and Applied Linguistics, Universiti Brunei Darussalam, vol. 7, 11-43. PDF from fass.ubd.edu.bn/staff/docs/AC/
catalog_locator: p.17 (p.7), section 'Stress.' under Phonology; also p.15 (gemination 'after a stressed syllable')
catalog_quote: Stress. There is no published description of stress patterns. Stress (in terms of intonational prominence and vowel length) appears to be generally penultimate bini-bini [...] ‘female’, banar [banar] ‘correct’. Final stress appears to be an optional pragmatic affect, restricted to utterance final contexts: a marked fall in pitch from a very high penultimate to a low utterance-final syllable, which is also often lengthened, e.g.: bulih! [bule:h] ‘(of course) you may!’, (s)udah! [uda:h] ‘already!’

audit.recode_to: no reclassification now. If Clynes 2014 drops the hedge (or Mataim 2007 states a rule) the record would move from 'undetermined' to penultimate (non-strict, with optional utterance-final prominence as a pragmatic effect), which Soderberg 2014 p.204 already asserts for the Kedayan dialect.
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim at Clynes 2001 printed p.17 = p.7 in the PDF we hold, txt and page scan; the p.15 gemination locator also checks. (2) Deciding source: a 2001 specialist overview/sketch, hedged twice; the held JIPA Illustration of Brunei Malay proper (Deterding & Ishamina 2017) has no stress section, and web searches (JIPA, Cambridge Elements, UBD FASS pages for Deterding/Ishamina/Clynes, general queries) found no instrumental or dedicated study of Brunei Malay word stress -- the instrumental Malay-stress literature is on Standard/Malaysian Malay or Standard Malay in Brunei. So Clynes 2001 is probably the best held-able source for Brunei Malay proper, and reading its hedged tendency as not determinable (penult tendency recorded in the primary-stress rule) is faithful. sources.citation: Soderberg, Craig D. 2014. Kedayan. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 44(2): 201-205 (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100314000061. Open access on Cambridge Core.
sources.quote: "Stress in Kedayan is predictable. Unaffixed words in isolation take primary stress on the penultimate syllable, e.g. [duˈii] 'thorn', [ˈaŋin] 'wind', [aˈkaa] 'root'." Speaker: Kedayan from Sipitang, Sabah (Malaysia); Kedayan (ISO kxd shared with Brunei Malay) is Glottolog dialect keda1250 under brun1242; author reports 83-89% lexical similarity to Brunei Malay.
sources.note: JIPA Illustration for the Kedayan dialect (Glottolog keda1250 under brun1242) with an unhedged penultimate-stress statement (p.204); the only firm positional statement for any brun1242 variety. downloaded now.
sources.venue: Journal of the International Phonetic Association

tone.quote: This paper describes the pronunciation of Kedayan, a minority indigenous language spoken in Brunei Darussalam that is closely related to Brunei Malay. Kedayan has 17 consonants and 3 vowels.

tone.quote: In addition to these 18 consonants, Jaludin ( Reference Chuchu 2000 : 154) lists the glottal stop /ʔ/ as a consonant of Brunei Malay, though Jaludin ( Reference Chuchu 2003 : 44) omits it. Poedjosoedarmo ( Reference Poedjosoedarmo 1996 : 40) notes that a glottal stop tends to be appended to word-final vowels in utterance-final position to indicate stress, in which case it is non-contrastive. It is therefore not listed as a phoneme here.
tone.summary: No lexical tone described; no prosody section; only an utterance-final glottal-stop 'stress' remark cited from Poedjosoedarmo 1996.
